title: Cherry-Picking
hook: A perfect set of facts can be dishonest when the missing cases are doing the work.
counterintuition: A true fact can still mislead when it was selected to hide the rest; name cherry-picking, then add the omitted cases before approving the claim.
keyTakeaway: Cherry-picking turns selected facts into a false whole. Correct it by asking what was left out before the decision moves.

breakdown.fastRead: The critic panel sees five airport screens where the new scoring rule found late departures. Gail is ready to approve the rule because every selected case looks damning. Then she points to the airport board and asks for the flights that left on time, the flights that arrived late for unrelated reasons, and the routes not shown at all. One accurate example may still come from a crooked sample. Cherry-picking is not a lie about one cherry. It is picking the cherries and hiding the tree.
breakdown.deepRead:
Cherry-picking works because selected facts can be real. The late flights really happened. The glowing testimonials really came from customers. The court examples really contain mistakes. That truth makes the trap harder to resist, because the argument does not feel fake. It feels supported.

The correction is to ask for the search rule. Who was included? Who was excluded? What cases would count against the claim? A claim backed by ten examples is weak if the speaker inspected a thousand cases and kept only the ten that helped. A claim backed by three failures may be strong if those were the only three cases in the file.

The missing cases are part of the evidence.

A medical-device review shows the move. Yvette hears a vendor present four hospitals with clean adverse-event logs. The stainless tasting spoon beside the lunch trays clinks while the room relaxes. Before signing the pilot, she asks whether any hospitals stopped using the device, failed to report, or logged events under another code. She is not calling the four clean logs false. She will not let omitted cases disappear.

That is the practical skill: use cherry-picking as the warning label, then make the specific correction before the choice moves forward. Request the denominator, the rejected cases, the time period, the search terms, and the evidence that would have embarrassed the claim. Selected facts can inform you only after the selection method is visible.
breakdown.fullRead:
The court file schedule is stacked on Janice's desk at 4:20 p.m. A lawyer wants the judge to see three borrowers who missed payments after refinancing. The loan worksheet looks decisive until Janice asks for the borrowers who refinanced and stayed current, the ones denied refinancing, and the dates used to build the file. The selected facts do not vanish. They shrink to their proper size.

Cherry-picking is often more dangerous than open invention because it borrows the dignity of evidence. A false number can be checked. A true number, carefully chosen, can walk through the door with a clean face. That is why the move has to happen before the room commits: mark the selection, ask what was not picked, and make the decision wait for the omitted cases.

Ask yourself one question: if this claim were wrong, which facts would its defender quietly leave in the basket?

A short history of medicine makes the pressure vivid. Taking the Medicine notes that the harm from smoking can be roughly as large as the combined benefit of postwar medical advances. If you display only new drugs, better surgery, and longer survival charts, modern medicine looks like a clean triumph. Add smoking's damage and the story changes. The cure is not cynicism about medicine. The cure is refusing to let selected facts pretend to be the whole field.

You can see the same shape in forecasting. Odette reviews a soccer playoff rule after a club director shows every year when the higher seed advanced. The shipping manifest from a delayed equipment order lies on the table, absurdly out of place, but it helps her slow down. She asks for seasons when the higher seed lost, years with changed injury rules, and games excluded because the format was different. The forecast becomes less dramatic and more useful.

Do not let selected facts pretend to be the whole field.

The Bible can be cherry-picked into almost any argument if verses are lifted without the surrounding passage. A wine harvest comparison has the same temptation in smaller form. Mireille can choose two sunny weeks, one flattering critic quote, and one scoreboard still from a tasting contest to call the vintage exceptional. Or she can include rain weeks, spoiled lots, low-scoring panels, and the comparison years that make the claim honest. The second version may sell less loudly, but it gives the buyer a real choice.

The limit is that complete evidence is rarely available. You cannot inspect every case before ordering lunch, hiring a contractor, or voting on a budget. The rule is not to demand perfect completeness. The rule is to notice when someone is asking a few vivid facts to stand in for a whole field. When the stakes are high, ask for the denominator. When the stakes are modest, ask for one contrary case. When the claim arrives polished, ask how the cherries were picked.

A true fact can still be a crooked sample. The honest move is to put the basket on the table.

examples.title: Gail asks for the flights not shown
examples.scenario: The airport board dominates the critic panel room in Vancouver at 9:12 a.m. Gail must decide whether a new score should punish regional carriers. She marks cherry-picking on the score sheet, asks for on-time flights and excluded routes, and changes the vote from approval to a wider sample review.
examples.whatToDo: Ask for the flights omitted from the scoring sheet before accepting the pattern.
examples.whyItMatters: The late departures may be real, but they cannot represent the airline until the missing routes and clean departures are visible.

planSpec.domain: a critic panel score sheet applying Cherry-Picking under operational pressure

examples.title: Janice expands the court file
examples.scenario: "These three defaults prove the refinancing program failed," the clerk says in a Calgary court office at 4:20 p.m. Janice must decide whether to accept the file summary. She writes selected facts on the loan worksheet, adds current borrowers and denied applicants, and delays the ruling note until the full comparison is attached.
examples.whatToDo: Turn selected facts into a comparison set before letting the file guide the decision.
examples.whyItMatters: Three defaults can be important without proving the program failed. The missing borrowers decide what the examples mean.

planSpec.domain: a court file schedule applying Cherry-Picking under operational pressure

examples.title: Yvette checks the silent hospitals
examples.scenario: The tasting spoon clicks against a lunch tray in a Paris clinic conference room at 1:15 p.m. while a vendor displays four clean hospital logs. Yvette, the device-safety lead, must decide whether the clinic should buy the device. She circles omitted cases, asks for hospitals that quit the pilot or coded events elsewhere, and pauses the order in front of the surgeon.
examples.whatToDo: Ask whether clean logs exclude failed sites, silent sites, or differently coded harms.
examples.whyItMatters: Clean cases can be cherry-picked too. The safety claim needs the hospitals that make the product look worse.

planSpec.domain: a medical-device adverse-event log applying Cherry-Picking under operational pressure

examples.title: Mireille puts the rain weeks back
examples.scenario: You are holding the scoreboard still from a tasting contest in a Bordeaux cellar at noon while Mireille, the export manager, faces a choice. She must decide whether to call the vintage exceptional. She writes Bible beside the cherry-picked critic quote, adds rain weeks and spoiled lots, and changes the buyer sheet before it is printed.
examples.whatToDo: Add the context that selected quotes or verses would leave out.
examples.whyItMatters: A flattering fragment can be true and still distort the whole harvest. Context stops the fragment from ruling the sale.

planSpec.domain: a wine harvest comparison applying Cherry-Picking under operational pressure

examples.title: Odette tests the playoff sample
examples.scenario: It took Odette two seasons to notice that the playoff forecast used only years when favorites won. At a Marseille club office at 7:05 p.m., she must decide whether to back a new seeding rule. She marks forecasting on a shipping manifest, adds upset seasons and rule-change years, and changes the board slide.
examples.whatToDo: Include the seasons that would weaken the forecast before backing the rule.
examples.whyItMatters: A forecast built from friendly years is not a forecast. It is a selection story with missing losses.

planSpec.domain: a soccer playoff rule applying Cherry-Picking under operational pressure

examples.title: Olga reopens the news queue
examples.scenario: Which listener comments belong on air after a public-radio segment angers donors? Olga reviews the Toronto news queue at 6:35 p.m. after the ad mockup has already been approved. She marks cherry on the rundown, adds supportive and neutral calls, and changes the postmortem from outrage story to sample problem.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the loudest comments from the full response set before writing the lesson.
examples.whyItMatters: A few vivid comments can make the audience look more unified than it is. The postmortem needs the full queue.

planSpec.domain: a public-radio news queue applying Cherry-Picking under operational pressure

questions.prompt: In a cherry-picking case, a charity report highlights five families helped by a grant, all photographed during the best week of the program, it says nothing about the applicants rejected, families who left early, or months when results fell. What is the cherry-picking risk?
choices: True stories are being used as if they represent the whole program without showing the omitted cases.
Early months results fits the immediate pressure around best week program; hold helped grant photographed steady and test highlights five families later.
Report highlights five looks strong enough to guide families helped grant; photographed best week can wait unless program says nothing changes the stakes.
questions.explanation: The family stories may be true, but they were selected. The correction is to ask for rejected applicants, exits, weak months, and the denominator before judging the grant.
questions.whyItMatters: Cherry-Picking makes cherry-picking case feel more decisive than the record supports, and that misprices charity report in this scene. The correct move keepss the choice by true stories are being used as if they represent the whole program without showing.

questions.prompt: During a cherry-picking review, a sales director shows six accounts that grew after a new pricing script, the slide omits accounts that received the script and shrank, plus accounts that grew before the script existed. What should you ask before approving the rollout?
choices: Approving rollout exposed points toward a quicker call on pricing script slide; let accounts grew after stand until plus existed what contradicts it.
Ask for exposed and unexposed accounts, plus the rule used to select the six examples.
Director shows accounts looks strong enough to guide grew after pricing; script slide omits can wait unless received shrank plus changes the stakes.
questions.explanation: The right move exposes the selection method and omitted comparison groups. A slogan or inspiring story leaves the cherry-picking intact.
questions.whyItMatters: Cherry-Picking works by letting cherry-picking sales crowd out director shows, which can misreads the accounts grew decision. Ask for exposed and unexposed accounts, plus the rule used to select the six examples keeps the practical cost tied to evidence.

questions.prompt: When cherry-picking pressure appears, a candidate quotes three lines from a long policy hearing to prove that an opponent hates small businesses. The full transcript includes later support, exceptions, and a separate concern about tax fraud. Which response best corrects the error?
choices: Separate concern about fits the immediate pressure around opponent hates small; hold policy hearing prove steady and test three lines long later.
Quotes three lines looks strong enough to guide long policy hearing; prove opponent hates can wait unless small businesses full changes the stakes.
Read the surrounding transcript and ask which lines were left out of the selection.
questions.explanation: The quotes can be accurate and still selected to distort meaning. The correction is context and omitted lines, not dueling cherry-picked fragments.
questions.whyItMatters: Cherry-Picking turns appears candidate into a shortcut, so the room can overweights quotes three while missing lines long. Read the surrounding transcript and ask which lines were left out of the selection protects the decision from that drift.

questions.prompt: After cherry-picking risk surfaces, a hospital vendor says its device is safe because three trial sites reported no incidents, one site withdrew, two sites changed reporting systems, and the vendor does not mention them. What is the strongest next decision?
choices: Pause approval until withdrawn and differently coded sites are included in the adverse-event review.
Vendor says device looks strong enough to guide safe three trial; sites reported incidents can wait unless site withdrew changed changes the stakes.
Device safe three gives a practical reason for hospital vendor says; incidents site withdrew belongs after trial sites reported clarifies the result.
questions.explanation: The clean sites matter only after the omitted sites are visible. Immediate approval accepts the selection; automatic rejection replaces analysis with suspicion.
questions.whyItMatters: Cherry-Picking would push the hospital vendor case toward says device, creating a cost when safe three stays untested. The useful guardrail is to pause approval until withdrawn and differently coded sites are included in the adverse-event review.

questions.prompt: If cherry-picking reasoning takes over, a newsletter claims a forecasting model is brilliant by listing every year it called the winner correctly. It leaves out years it made no call, years it changed the call late, and years with changed rules. What makes this cherry-picking?
choices: Forecasting model brilliant gives a practical reason for reasoning newsletter claims; winner correctly leaves belongs after listing year called clarifies the result.
Brilliant listing year makes cherry-picking reasoning newsletter look credible; use claims forecasting model first and revisit called winner correctly when leaves years call shifts.
The successes were chosen without the full set of attempts and misses.
questions.explanation: The selected wins are not enough. Forecasting evidence needs the full attempt record, including no-calls, late changes, misses, and altered conditions.
questions.whyItMatters: Cherry-Picking converts claims forecasting into the loudest signal, which can rushes model brilliant before listing year is checked. The better answer separatess attention on the successes were chosen without the full set of attempts and misses.

questions.prompt: While cherry-picking pressure builds, a manager wants to fire a contractor after collecting three angry emails, the folder also holds twenty quiet renewals and four satisfied clients who never wrote. Which action keeps selected facts from driving the choice?
choices: Cherry-picking pressure builds looks strong enough to guide manager wants fire; contractor after collecting can wait unless three angry emails changes the stakes.
Compare angry emails with renewals, silent clients, and the total client count before deciding.
Angry emails folder makes wants fire contractor look credible; use after collecting three first and revisit also holds twenty when quiet renewals four shifts.
questions.explanation: The angry emails may point to a problem, but the decision needs the omitted cases and denominator. Deleting them hides evidence in the opposite direction.
questions.whyItMatters: Cherry-Picking hides inside the cherry-picking pressure choice because cherry-picking pressure seems sufficient, yet the cost lands in cherry-picking pressure. Compare angry emails with renewals, silent clients, and the total client count before deciding brings the cherry-picking pressure comparison back.

questions.prompt: Before the cherry-picking call, a nutrition influencer shows only blood-test panels from followers whose marker improved after buying a supplement. You are reviewing an ad claim before it goes live. Which question should block the claim until answered?
choices: Cherry-picking call nutrition looks strong enough to guide influencer shows blood-test; panels followers whose can wait unless marker improved after changes the stakes.
How many followers tested, how many did not improve, and how were the displayed panels chosen?
Improved after buying makes shows blood-test panels look credible; use followers whose marker first and revisit supplement claim goes when live block until shifts.
questions.explanation: Cherry-picking hides in the selection rule. The ad needs the full test group and non-improvers, not better packaging around selected panels.
questions.whyItMatters: Cherry-Picking pressures the call nutrition decision toward the easy reading of call nutrition. That can inflates the real cost unless the choice is grounded in how many followers tested, how many did not improve, and how were the displayed panels.

questions.prompt: Suppose cherry-picking risk is present: a school district promotes a reading program using only classrooms taught by its two most experienced teachers. It omits new teachers, classrooms that dropped the program, and schools with low attendance. What is the most precise diagnosis?
choices: What precise diagnosis points toward a quicker call on program classrooms taught; let district promotes reading stand until dropped schools attendance contradicts it.
Diagnosis selected flatter fits the immediate pressure around taught experienced teachers; hold reading program classrooms steady and test school district promotes later.
The case set was selected to flatter the program, so omitted classrooms must be added.
questions.explanation: The problem is not simply noise. The district chose favorable classrooms and left out cases that could weaken the conclusion.
questions.whyItMatters: Cherry-Picking is the mechanism here: selected evidence poses as the whole record, so present school can overpower present school. The case set was selected to flatter the program, so omitted classrooms must be added keeps the scenario from becoming a.

questions.prompt: Two cherry-picking signals compete: a board packet uses three disaster stories to argue against expanding a ferry schedule. The packet excludes years when expanded schedules worked, weather differences, and maintenance periods. What is the cleanest correction?
choices: Build a table with all expanded-schedule years, conditions, failures, and successes before voting.
Expanding ferry schedule supports a narrower read of signals compete board; keep packet three disaster central and leave stories argue against aside.
Schedule excludes years points toward a quicker call on board packet three; let cherry-picking signals compete stand until against expanding ferry contradicts it.
questions.explanation: The correction is the full field of cases with conditions attached. Counter-cherry-picking with success stories would repeat the same error.
questions.whyItMatters: Cherry-Picking makes the board packet evidence look cleaner than it is, risking a board packet mistake in this setting. The answer protects board packet by asking for build a table with all expanded-schedule years, conditions, failures, and successes before voting.

reviewCards.front: A claim is backed by vivid true examples. What omitted cases should be requested?
reviewCards.back: Request the failures, near misses, excluded cases, and denominator. True examples need the cases they left out.

reviewCards.front: Someone shows successes but not attempts. What is the missing check?
reviewCards.back: Ask for the denominator, the selection rule, and the failures that would weaken the claim.

reviewCards.front: A quote, chart, or testimonial feels decisive. What makes it honest?
reviewCards.back: It becomes useful only when the surrounding context and contrary cases are visible.

reviewCards.front: A forecast lists only its wins. What should you ask for?
reviewCards.back: Ask for misses, no-calls, changed calls, and excluded periods before trusting the pattern.

reviewCards.front: You cannot get the full dataset. What is the smaller correction?
reviewCards.back: Ask for one contrary case and one reason the displayed examples were selected.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Treat selected facts as a warning to ask for omitted cases before deciding.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a deck uses examples to prove a claim, then I will ask for the cases that would weaken it.
If a model lists wins, then I will ask for attempts, misses, no-calls, and changed calls.
If testimonials drive a purchase or policy, then I will ask how they were chosen and who was excluded.
If a quote feels decisive, then I will read the surrounding context before using it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Take one claim you heard today that uses examples. Write the selection rule you would need and one omitted case that could change your mind.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, audit one persuasive chart or story by adding a denominator, contrary cases, and excluded periods.

tryThisNow: Take one claim backed by examples. Write the excluded cases you would expect to see if the claim were honest, then ask for them before deciding.
